record.paper_title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems
record.original_question: Can the canonical method determine the QCD critical point and first-order transition structure on substantially larger lattices with controlled errors, rather than only on the small volumes used in existing successful studies? This includes whether canonical calculations can overcome the growing sign problem and computational cost enough to make their current critical-point claims robust in larger-volume regimes.

evidence.quote: To study the first-order phase transition line, it is necessary to increase the density at the temperature corresponding to the hadron phase. In that case, the problem is how well this phase fluctuation is under control.

Probably, the most successful approach so far is the canonical method, with which multiple groups reported the discovery of the QCD critical point. However, all simulations were performed on small lattice sizes, and it is important to go to a larger lattice size.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at finite baryon density studied via the canonical ensemble method. In this approach one fixes the net quark (or baryon) number N and computes the canonical partition function Z_C(N,T,V) by Fourier-transforming the grand-canonical partition function in the imaginary chemical potential μ = iθT:
   Z_C(N,T,V) = (1/2π) ∫_{-π}^{π} dθ e^{-iNθ} Z_GC(iθT, T, V),
where Z_GC is evaluated by standard Monte Carlo simulation at imaginary chemical potential (where the fermion determinant is real and the sign problem is absent). Observables at real chemical potential μ_B are reconstructed via fugacity expansion Z_GC(μ_B,T,V) = Σ_N Z_C(N,T,V) e^{N μ_B/T}. By searching for an S-shaped structure (Maxwell construction) in the chemical-potential–density relation, one attempts to locate the QCD critical end point and the first-order chiral/deconfinement transition line in the (T, μ_B) plane.

Existing successful canonical-method studies that have reported a QCD critical point have all used small spatial lattice volumes. The question is the following:

Can the canonical method determine the QCD critical end point and the structure of the first-order transition line on substantially larger spatial lattices (taking the thermodynamic limit under control) with quantitatively controlled statistical and systematic errors? In particular, can the canonical-method computation overcome:
(i) the residual/oscillatory sign problem arising from rapid phase fluctuations of the integrand e^{-iNθ} Z_GC(iθT) at large N, especially in the hadronic/confined phase, and
(ii) the growing computational cost of accurately determining Z_C(N,T,V) for the range of N relevant to the first-order transition,
to the extent that current critical-point claims become robust as the lattice volume is increased toward the thermodynamic limit?
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (through 2025) continues to treat the QCD critical point search via the canonical method as an active, unresolved problem. Existing canonical-method critical-point studies remain on small lattices, and known phase-fluctuation issues in the canonical approach (a residual sign problem at large N) and computational cost still limit reliable extension to larger volumes. Recent work (e.g., 2025 lattice constraints on the critical point via improved equations of state) addresses related questions but does not establish a controlled-error canonical determination of the critical point on substantially larger lattices.

status_evidence.title: Lattice QCD constraints on the critical point from an improved precision equation of state
status_evidence.snippet: Lattice simulations to search for the critical point of QCD by following contours of constant entropy density from imaginary to real chemical potentials.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2025, the QCD critical point location is still being constrained by lattice methods rather than definitively determined.

status_evidence.title: Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: Current status and open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Canonical method critical-point claims rely on small lattices; extension to larger volumes is listed among open problems.
status_evidence.claim: Larger-volume canonical-method critical-point determinations remain identified as open.

status_evidence.title: Use of the canonical approach in effective models of QCD
status_evidence.snippet: The canonical approach may suffer from a new type of sign problem: phases proportional to N fluctuate rapidly at large N, particularly in the confined phase, limiting accessible N.
status_evidence.claim: A residual sign problem in the canonical method limits its applicability at the large-N values needed for studying the first-order transition.
